rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ❌ Heat capacity and specific heat are the same thing. ✅ Heat capacity ($C'$) depends on the object's mass; specific heat ($c$) is a property of the material alone. $C' = mc$ - they are related but not identical.  ·  ❌ A larger object always has a larger heat capacity. ✅ For the SAME material, yes. But a small lead weight ($c=130$) may have a smaller $C'$ than a large aluminum block ($c=900$) even if the lead is more massive.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: ❌ Heat capacity has no units. ✅ Heat capacity has units: J/K (SI) or cal/°C (CGS). Specific heat has units J/kg·K or cal/g·°C. The units are different by a factor of mass.  ·  ❌ Heat capacity is the same for all objects of the same material. ✅ Heat capacity depends on BOTH material and mass. Two copper objects have the same $c$ but different $C'$ if their masses differ.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: **Definition:** Heat capacity (also called thermal capacity), denoted $C'$ or simply $C$, is the amount of heat energy required to raise the temperature of an **entire object** (not a unit mass) by 1 K (or 1°C).  ·  **Formula:** $C' = m \cdot c$, where $m$ is the mass of the object and $c$ is the specific heat capacity of the material. Alternatively, $C' = H/\Delta\theta$ - heat required per degree of temperature rise.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Heat capacity is sometimes called "thermal mass" in engineering. A brick wall has high thermal mass - it absorbs heat during the day and releases it at night, moderating indoor temperatures.  ·  The concept of heat capacity was developed by Joseph Black in the 1760s. rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Heat exchanged using C':** $H = C' \cdot \Delta\theta$. This is simpler than $H = mc\Delta\theta$ when you already know the heat capacity of the object.  ·  **SI unit:** $\text{J/K}$ (joule per kelvin) or $\text{J/°C}$. Since a kelvin and a degree Celsius have the same size, $\text{J/K} = \text{J/°C}$ numerically.  ·  **CGS unit:** $\text{cal/°C}$ (calorie per degree Celsius). Water's heat capacity is $1\text{ cal/°C}$ per gram, or $4.186\text{ J/°C}$ per gram.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ The dimensional formula of heat capacity is $[M^0L^2T^{-2}\Theta^{-1}]$. ✅ Heat capacity includes mass: $[C'] = [ML^2T^{-2}\Theta^{-1}]$. The $[M]$ does NOT cancel because $C'$ depends on the amount of substance.  ·  ❌ You can use $C'$ in place of $c$ in all formulas. ✅ In $H = mc\Delta\theta$, replace $mc$ with $C'$: $H = C'\Delta\theta$. But if you need $c$ itself (e.g., to identify the material), you must divide: $c = C'/m$.  ·  ❌ Water equivalent has units of J/K. ✅ Water equivalent ($W$) has units of MASS (kg or g). Heat capacity has units of J/K. They are related by $C' = W \cdot c_w$, where $c_w = 4186\text{ J/kg·K}$.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Statement 5: Corollary or consequence of Heat Capacity (Thermal Capacity, C′)  ·  A 2 kg iron block ($c = 450\text{ J/kg·K}$) is heated from 20°C to 80°C. Find its heat capacity and the heat required. $C' = 2 \times 450 = 900\text{ J/K}$. $H = 900 \times 60 = 54{,}000\text{ J} = 54\text{ kJ}$.  ·  An object has heat capacity 840 J/K. How much heat raises its temperature by 15°C? $H = C'\Delta\theta = 840 \times 15 = 12{,}600\text{ J} = 12.6\text{ kJ}$.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: A calorimeter has mass 0.05 kg and $c = 400\text{ J/kg·K}$. Find its heat capacity and water equivalent. $C' = 0.05 \times 400 = 20\text{ J/K}$. $W = C'/c_w = 20/4186 = 0.00478\text{ kg} = 4.78\text{ g}$.  ·  Two objects A and B have the same heat capacity. Object A is 0.5 kg of aluminum ($c=900$). Object B is 1.0 kg of an unknown material. Find B's specific heat. $C'_A = 0.5 \times 900 = 450\text{ J/K}$. Since $C'_B = C'_A$: $1.0 \times c_B = 450 \Rightarrow c_B = 450\text{ J/kg·K}$ (iron).  ·  A copper calorimeter ($m = 0.1\text{ kg}$, $c = 390$) contains 0.2 kg of water. Find the total heat capacity of the system. $C'_{cal} = 0.1 \times 390 = 39\text{ J/K}$. $C'_{water} = 0.2 \times 4200 = 840\text{ J/K}$. $C'_{total} = 39 + 840 = 879\text{ J/K}$.
